label: Compressed gas
summary: Gas cylinders and air tanks hold huge stored energy. A snapped valve can turn a cylinder into a rocket. Nitrogen and argon push air out of closed spaces; CO2 is toxic itself and can kill with normal oxygen. Oxygen makes grease and clothing burn fiercely. Propane and acetylene burn and explode.
signs: Steel or aluminium cylinders with a valve on top: welding, medical, propane, CO2, diving and nitrogen
Drink-dispensing CO2 bottles in bars and restaurants: leaked CO2 is 1.5 times heavier than air and pools at floor level in basements and other low rooms, even away from the bottle
Hissing, frost on a valve, or a fallen cylinder
Cylinder colours vary by country: read the label, not the paint

Cylinders and aerosol cans left in a closed car in summer: aerosols should stay under 50 °C and cylinders under 52 °C, and one test cited by the Canada Safety Council had a parked car pass 50 °C in 20 minutes on a 35 °C day. Heat can burst them. Collect them in spring or autumn.
do: Keep cylinders upright and strapped or chained so they can't fall
Keep the valve cap on when moving a cylinder
Open valves slowly, standing to the side of the outlet
Check fittings for leaks with soapy water
Store cylinders outdoors or somewhere ventilated, in shade, away from heat
Air out basements and low rooms where gas bottles are kept before going in: draw air out low and let fresh air in high. An oxygen reading alone doesn't clear a CO2 room
dont: Don't drop a cylinder, roll it by the valve, or hit it
Don't heat a cylinder or leave it in a hot vehicle
Don't put oil or grease on oxygen fittings
Don't cut, drill or weld a cylinder or tank, even an 'empty' one
Don't rush in to help someone who collapsed in a basement or closed room: you will collapse too
Don't loosen a regulator, hose or fitting while there is pressure behind it: close the valve and bleed the pressure off first
ppe: Gloves; escaping gas can freeze skin
firstAid: Collapse in a low or closed space: ventilate first and rescue from outside if you can, then start CPR if they aren't breathing

Cold burns from escaping gas: the Emergency Response Guidebook says only medical personnel should thaw frosted skin. With none to hand, and only if it can't refreeze, soak it in 37–39 °C water for about 30 minutes; don't rub. Blisters or numbness need medical care (see Cold)
Hit by a cylinder or fitting: control bleeding, splint suspected broken bones, and get medical help
